¶
'''wheezily''' (hwē′zi-li), ''adv.'' In a wheezing manner; as if with difficulty of breathing.
{{smaller block|“The potman was a-listening,” he said, ''wheezily''; “I could see it by the way he ’eld ’is ’ed.”
{{right|''D. Christie Murray'', Weaker Vessel, xii.}}}}

'''wheezy''' (hwē′zi), ''a.'' [< ''wheeze'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Affected with or characterized by wheezing.
{{smaller block|So Fred was gratified with nearly an hour’s practice of . . . favorite airs from his “Instructor on the Flute”—a ''wheezy'' performance, into which he threw much ambition and an irrepressible hopefulness.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, xi.}}}}

'''wheft''' (hweft), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', an erroneous form of ''waft'', 4.

'''whelk'''<sup>1</sup> (hwelk), ''n.'' [< ME. ''whelke'', ''qwelke'', dim. of ''wheal''<sup>1</sup>.] A wheal; a pustule; a swelling or protuberance, as on the body.
{{smaller block|<poem>Boras, ceruce, ne oille of tartre noon,
Ne oynement that wolde clense and byte,
That him mighte helpen of his ''whelkes'' whyte.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 632.}}
One Bardolph, if your majesty know the man; his face is all bubukles, and ''whelks'', and knobs, and flames o’ fire.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iii. 6. 108.}}}}

''wiloc'', later ''weoluc'', ''weluc'', a mollusk with a spiral or convoluted shell, prob. orig. *''wilc'', < ''wealcan'', roll, walk: see ''walk'', ''v.''] A gastropod of the family ''Buccinidæ'' in a broad sense; a buccinid, or some similar univalve with a spi-
readings.c2s3:
''welked'', early mod. E. ''wealked''; < ''whelk''<sup>2</sup>, ''welk''<sup>3</sup>, + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Formed like a whelk; hence, marked or covered with ridges like those of a whelk.

{{smaller block|Horns ''whelk’d'' [var. ''welk’d'', ''wealk’d''] and waved like the enridged sea.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 6. 71.}}}}

{{smaller block|Look up at its [the tree’s] towering expanse of branches, observe its ''whelked'' and furrowed bole, and try to clasp it round.
{{right|''A. S. Palmer'', Word Hunter’s Note-Book, iv.}}}}

'''whelk-tingle''' (hwelk′tin″gl), ''n.'' A kind of dog-whelk, ''Nassa reticulata'', common on the English coast. See cut under ''dog-whelk''. [Eng.]

'''whelky<sup>1</sup>†''' (hwel′ki), ''a.'' [< ''whelk''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Abounding in whelks, pustules, or blisters.

{{smaller block|Pluck . . . stood sunk to his chin in the snow, and laughed as heartily as any of them, his shining bald pate and ''whelky'' red face streaming with moisture and shaking with merriment.
{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, i. 17.}}}}

'''whelky<sup>2</sup>''' (hwel′ki), ''a.'' [Prop. ''welky''; < ''whelk''<sup>2</sup>, + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Formed like a whelk; hence, knobby; rounded.

{{smaller block|<poem>Ne ought the ''whelky'' pearles esteemeth hee,
Which are from Indian seas brought far away.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Virgil’s Gnat, l. 105.}}}}

'''whelm''' (hwelm), ''v.'' [< ME. ''whelmen'', an altered form (due to the influence of the different word ''welm'', or a lost noun, *''whelm'' for *''whelfm'') of ''whelven'', turn, overturn, cover by something turned over, overwhelm, = OS. ''be-hwelbian'' = D. ''welven'' = MHG. ''welben'', G. ''wölben'', arch over, cover, = Icel. ''hvālfa'', ''hōlfa'', turn upside down, = Sw. ''hvälfva'' = Dan. ''hvælve'', arch over; associated with AS. ''hwealf'', arched, convex, ''hwealf'', a vault, = Icel. ''hvālf'', ''hōlf'', a vault, arch, = Sw.

{{smaller|strict the name ''wheel-window'' to examples in which straight}} spokes are particularly suggested. Also called ''catharine-wheel''.
{{smaller block|The transept façade has sometimes a ''wheel window'' at the clerestory level, as at Lincoln, and sometimes it has such a window in the gable, as at York and Beverley.

'''wheelwork''' (hwēl′wėrk), ''n.'' A combination of wheels, as in watches and clocks, in embroidery, etc.

'''wheel-worn''' (hwēl′wōrn), ''a.'' Worn by the action of moving wheels.
{{smaller block|The chariots abounding in her ''wheel-worn'' streets.
{{right|''Cowper'', Expostulation, l. 21.}}}}

'''wheelwright''' (hwēl′rīt), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whelwriȝt'', ''qwelwriȝte''; < ''wheel''<sup>1</sup> + ''wright''.]   A person who works at or with a wheel; specifically, a man whose occupation is to make wheels, wheeled carriages, etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>A wifman of so much myȝth,
So wonder a ''whelwryȝth'',
Sey I nevere with syȝth.</poem>
{{right|''MS. Laud.'' 108, fol. 237 (Rel. Antiq., II. 8).}}}}
{{smaller block|The basket-maker peeling his willow wands in the sunshine; the ''wheelwright'' putting the last touch to a blue cart with red wheels.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, Int.}}}}

'''Wheelwrights’ machine''', {{smaller|an adjustable machine for doing some of the various operations by which a wagon-wheel is made, as boring the hubs and fellies and tenoning the spokes.}}

'''wheely''' (hwē′li), ''a.''   [< ''wheel''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Circular; suitable to rotation.
{{smaller block|<poem>Give a ''wheely'' form
To the expected grinder.</poem>
{{right|''J. Philips'', Cider, ii.}}}}

'''wheen'''<sup>1</sup> (hwēn), ''n.''   [Also ''whin''; < ME. *''whene'', < AS. ''hwǣne'', ''hwēne''; secondary form of ME. ''whon'', ''qwon'', ''hwan'', ''hwon'', ''wan'', < AS. ''hwōn'', adv., a little, somewhat.]   A little (originally used adverbially); a small number; hence, a quantity. [Scotch.]

{{smaller block|There will be a ''wheen'' idle gowks coming to glower at the hole as lang as it is daylight.
{{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, xxiv.}}}}

'''wheen<sup>2</sup>''' (hwēn), ''n.'' A dialectal form of ''queen''<sup>1</sup>.

<poem>That es called the ''wheene'' of Amazonnes,
Undyr whose powere that folk wonnes.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Hampole.'' (''Halliwell.'')}}}}

'''wheen-cat''' (hwēn′kat), ''n.''   [< ''wheen''<sup>2</sup> + ''cat''<sup>1</sup>.]   A queen or female cat.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''wheeze''' (hwēz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''wheezed'', ppr. ''wheezing''.   [Formerly also ''wheaze''; < ME. ''hwesen'', < AS. ''hwēsan'' (pret. ''hweós''), wheeze; perhaps akin to Icel. ''hvæsa'' = Sw. ''hväsa'' = Dan. ''hvæse'', hiss, wheeze, and to the imitative E. words, ''whisper'', ''whistle''. Cf. Skt. √ ''çvas'', puff, breathe, L. ''queri'' (pp. ''questus''), complain: see ''quest''<sup>1</sup>, ''querulous''. For the alleged connection with ''weasand'', see ''weasand''.]   To breathe hard; puff and blow; breathe with difficulty and audibly.

{{smaller block|Catarrhs, . . . ''wheezing'' lungs.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., v. 1. 24.}}}}

{{smaller block|The patient [in asthma] . . . begins to ''wheeze'' during sleep, and is only aroused when the dyspnœa becomes severe.
{{right|''Quain'', Med. Dict., p. 91.}}}}

'''wheeze''' (hwēz), ''n.''   [< ''wheeze'', ''v.'']   A puffing or blowing, especially as in labored breathing.

{{smaller block|The fat old dog on the portico gave a gentle ''wheeze'' of recognition.
{{right|''The Atlantic'', LXVI. 185.}}}}

'''wheezily''' (hwē′zi-li), ''adv.'' In a wheezing manner; as if with difficulty of breathing.
{{smaller block|“The potman was a-listening,” he said, ''wheezily''; “I could see it by the way he ’eld ’is ’ed.”
{{right|''D. Christie Murray'', Weaker Vessel, xii.}}}}

{{right|''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, xi.}}}}

'''wheft''' (hweft), ''n.''   ''Naut.'', an erroneous form of ''waft'', 4.

'''whelk'''<sup>1</sup> (hwelk), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whelke'', ''qwelke'', dim. of ''wheal''<sup>1</sup>.]   A wheal; a pustule; a swelling or protuberance, as on the body.
{{smaller block|<poem>Boras, ceruce, ne oille of tartre noon,
Ne oynement that wolde clense and byte,
That him mighte helpen of his ''whelkes'' whyte.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 632.}}}}
{{smaller block|One Bardolph, if your majesty know the man; his face is all bubukles, and ''whelks'', and knobs, and flames o’ fire.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iii. 6. 108.}}}}

'''whelk'''<sup>2</sup> (hwelk), ''n.''   [An erroneous modern form of ''welk''<sup>3</sup>, < ME. ''welk'', ''wilk'', ''wylke'' (> OF. ''welke''), < AS. ''wiloc'', later ''weoluc'', ''weluc'', a mollusk with a spiral or convoluted shell, prob. orig. *''wilc'', < ''wealcan'', roll, walk: see ''walk'', ''v.'']   A gastropod of the family ''Buccinidæ'' in a broad sense; a buccinid, or some similar univalve with a spiral gibbous shell whose aperture forms a kind of spout, and whose whorls are more or less varicose or whelked. {{smaller|A very common whelk to which the name may have originally or especially applied is ''Buccinum undatum''. See also cuts under ''Buccinum'', ''cancrisocial'', ''nidamental'', ''ribbon'', and ''Siphonostomata''. Also ''wilk''.}}
{{smaller block|A deal table, on which are exposed . . . oysters . . . and divers specimens of a species of snail (''wilks'', we think they are called), floating in a somewhat bilious-looking green liquid. {{right|''Dickens'', Sketches, Scenes, xii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Live ''whelks'', the lips’-beard dripping fresh,
As if they still the water’s lisp heard.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Popularity.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''whelk'' and barnacle are clinging to the hardened sand. {{right|''Geikie'', Geol. Sketches, ii.}}}}
'''Reversed whelk''', {{smaller|''Fulgur perversa''.}}—'''Ribbon whelk''', {{smaller|one of the large whelks which spin out a ribbon or ruffle of egg-cases, as ''Fulgur'' (or ''Busycon'') ''carica'' and ''Sycotypus canaliculatus''; a hairy whelk. [Local, U. S.]}}—'''Rough whelk''', {{smaller|''Urosalpinx cinerea'', the borer or drill. See cut under ''Urosalpinx''. (See also ''dog-whelk''.)}}

'''whelked''' (hwelkt), ''a.''   [An erroneous form of ''welked'', early mod. E. ''wealked''; < ''whelk''<sup>2</sup>, ''welk''<sup>3</sup>, + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Formed like a whelk; hence, marked or covered with ridges like those of a whelk.

{{smaller block|Horns ''whelk’d'' [var. ''welk’d'', ''wealk’d''] and waved like the enridged sea.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 6. 71.}}}}

{{smaller block|Look up at its [the tree’s] towering expanse of branches, observe its ''whelked'' and furrowed bole, and try to clasp it round.
{{right|''A. S. Palmer'', Word Hunter’s Note-Book, iv.}}}}

'''whelk-tingle''' (hwelk′tin″gl), ''n.'' A kind of dog-whelk, ''Nassa reticulata'', common on the English coast. See cut under ''dog-whelk''. [Eng.]

'''whelky<sup>1</sup>†''' (hwel′ki), ''a.''   [< ''whelk''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Abounding in whelks, pustules, or blisters.

{{smaller block|Pluck . . . stood sunk to his chin in the snow, and laughed as heartily as any of them, his shining bald pate and ''whelky'' red face streaming with moisture and shaking with merriment.
{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, i. 17.}}}}

'''whelky<sup>2</sup>''' (hwel′ki), ''a.''   [Prop. ''welky''; < ''whelk''<sup>2</sup>, + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Formed like a whelk; hence, knobby; rounded.

<poem>Ne ought the ''whelky'' pearles esteemeth hee,
Which are from Indian seas brought far away.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Spenser'', Virgil’s Gnat, l. 105.}}}}

'''whelm''' (hwelm), ''v.''   [< ME. ''whelmen'', an altered form (due to the influence of the different word ''welm'', or a lost noun, *''whelm'' for *''whelfm'') of ''whelven'', turn, overturn, cover by something turned over, overwhelm, = OS. ''be-hwelbian'' = D. ''welven'' = MHG. ''welben'', G. ''wölben'', arch over, cover, = Icel. ''hvālfa'', ''hōlfa'', turn upside down, = Sw. ''hvälfva'' = Dan. ''hvælve'', arch over; associated with AS. ''hwealf'', arched, convex, ''hwealf'', a vault, = Icel. ''hvālf'', ''hōlf'', a vault, arch, = Sw. hvalf = Dan. ''hvælv'', a vault, arch; cf. Gr. κόλπος, bosom, gulf (see ''gulf'').]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To throw over so as to cover. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|I ''whelme'' an hollowe thyng over an other thyng. Je met dessus. . . . ''Whelme'' a platter upon it, to save it from flyes.
{{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 780.}}}}
{{smaller block|Hill upon hill ''whelmed'' upon it [the church], nay, [it lay] like a grain of corn between the upper and lower mill-stone, ground to dust between tyrants and heretics.
{{right|''Donne'', Sermons, xvii.}}}}
'''2.''' To engulf; submerge; cover by immersion in something that envelops on all sides; overwhelm.
{{smaller block|<poem>She is my prize, or ocean ''whelm'' them all.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 2. 143.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>We perish’d, each alone;
But I beneath a rougher sea,
And ''whelm’d'' in deeper gulfs than he.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', The Cast-away.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Drawn thro’ either chasm . . .
Roll’d a sea-haze, and ''whelm’d'' the world in gray.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}}}
'''3.''' Hence, to crush, ruin, or destroy by some sudden overpowering disaster.
{{smaller block|<poem>Grievous mischiefes which a wicked Fay
Had wrought, and many ''whelmd'' in deadly paine.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ii. 43.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To ''whelm''
All of them in one massacre.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lucretius.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To pass or roll over so as to cover or submerge.
{{smaller block|The waves ''whelm’d'' over him.
{{right|''Dryden'', Don Sebastian, i. 1.}}}}

'''whelp''' (hwelp), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whelp'', ''welp'', ''hweolp'', ''hwelp'', < AS. ''hwelp'' = OS. ''hwelp'' = D. ''welp'' = LG. ''welp'' = OHG. ''hwelf'', ''welf'', MHG. ''welf'' = Icel. ''hvelpr'' = OSw. ''hwalp'', Sw. ''valp'' = Dan. ''hvalp'', a whelp, the young of dogs, wolves, lions, and other beasts.]   '''1.''' The young of the dog, wolf, lion, tiger, bear, seal, etc., but especially of the dog; a cub: sometimes applied to the whole canine species, whether young or old.
{{smaller block|The Liun of Prude [Pride] haueth swuthe monie ''hweolpes.''
{{right|''Ancren Riwle'', p. 198.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Youre rede colera, parde,
Which causeth folk to dremen in here dremes . . .
Of grete bestes, that they wol hem byte,
Of contek, and of ''whelpes'' grete and lyte.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Nun’s Priest’s Tale, l. 112.}}}}
{{smaller block|A bear robbed of her ''whelps.'' {{right|2 Sam. xvii. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The son [Caliban] that she did litter here,
A freckled ''whelp'' hag-born. ''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 283.</poem>
<poem>Both mongrel, puppy, ''whelp'', and hound,
And curs of low degree.</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Elegy on Death of a Mad Dog.}}}}
'''2.''' A youth; a cub; a puppy: a term of contempt.
{{smaller block|On one of the back benches . . . sat the villainous ''whelp'', sulky to the last, whom he had the misery to call his son. {{right|''Dickens'', Hard Times, iii. 7.}}}}
'''3†.''' A kind of ship.
{{smaller block|25 July, 1635. About six hour I went aboard one of the king’s ships called the ninth ''whelp'', which is in the king’s books 215 ton and tonnage in king’s books. She carries sixteen pieces of ordinance. . . . This ship is manned with sixty men. {{right|''Brereton'', Travels, p. 164. (''Davies.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|Four of the king’s ships and six merchant ships are to go for the coast of Ireland, to beat the Turks thence. And the occasion was this: Captain Plumley was sent thither with one of the ships royal and two ''whelps'' to seek out Nutt the pirate.
{{right|''Court and Times of Charles I.'', II. 186.}}}}
'''4.''' ''Naut.'', one of several longitudinal projections from the barrel of a capstan, windlass, or winch, provided to take the strain of the chain or rope which is being hove upon, and afford a firmer hold.—'''5.''' One of the teeth of a sprocket-wheel.   ''E. H. Knight.''

'''whelp''' (hwelp), ''v.''   [Also Sc. ''whalp''; < ME. ''whelpen'', ''hwelpen'', ''hweolpen''; < ''whelp'', ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To bring forth young, as the female of the dog and various beasts of prey.
{{smaller block|They [sharks] spawne not, but ''whelp'', like the Dogge or Wolfe, and at night or towardes stormes receiue their young into their mouthes for safetie.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 902.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is a Bitch-otter, and she has lately ''whelp’d''.
{{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 60.}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' To bring forth, as a bitch, lioness, and many beasts of prey; hence, to give birth to; originate: used in contempt.
{{smaller block|Then said Lycurgus, you are witnesses that these two dogges were ''whelpt'' in one day, . . . of one syre and dam.
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 22.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Did thy foul fancy ''whelp'' so foul a scheme
Of hopes abortive?</poem>
{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, vii. 901.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He was nane o’ Scotland’s dogs,
But ''whalpit'' some place far abroad,
Whare sailors gang to fish for cod.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', The Twa Dogs.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
